Even if you halved CAC to ₹221, you'd still be at ₹1,100 × 24% − ₹221 = +₹43 — wafer-thin, one return or one COD reject and you're underwater again.

The disease here isn't the ads, it's a 24% gross margin. At that margin there is no keyword tweak, no match-type change, no LP optimisation that makes the unit economics work — the maths simply doesn't have room. CAC ₹442 against a ₹264 gross profit per order is the tell.

So the lever sits upstream of marketing entirely: fix the margin. Renegotiate COGS, raise price, or lift AOV with bundles/refills so each order carries enough gross profit to pay for acquisition and leave a cushion. Get gross margin toward 40%+ and suddenly ₹442 CAC is fine.

Caveat — I'm reading one 30-day window. If this is a first-order-only number and your 90-day repeat is genuinely strong, LTV could rescue it. But you didn't mention repeat, which makes me think it isn't carrying you. Pull repeat rate before you touch the ad account.

an0909.user: Quick one on my coffee brand. I've been running Meta for the past week — spent about ₹32K, got 22 conversions so far. I want to know if my CAC is good and whether I should pour more budget in or just kill it. Trying not to waste money either way.
an0909.assistant:
Honest answer: you can't know yet, and anyone who gives you a confident read off this is guessing.

22 conversions over 7 days is far too small a sample to conclude anything. Whatever CAC you calculate — ₹32K ÷ 22 ≈ ₹1,455 — has huge error bars around it. Three good days or three bad days swing that number wildly. Scaling or killing on this is a coin flip dressed up as a decision.

Let it run until you've got roughly 100 conversions, or a clean 2–3 week window, whichever comes first. At ~100 the CAC stabilises enough to actually trust. Don't touch budget, don't touch targeting in the meantime — you'll only add noise and reset the learning.

The one discipline here: stop checking it daily. Set the threshold (100 conversions) and look again then. That's the whole answer for now.

an0910.user: Right, my Amazon Ads CTR for the salon chain just dropped 13% versus last week and I'm ready to tear the whole strategy down and rebuild — new creatives, new keywords, the works. We did 63 conversions this week. Where do I even start the overhaul?
an0910.assistant:
Start by doing nothing. Put the rebuild plans down.

A 13% CTR move week-over-week on 63 conversions is well inside normal variance — that's not a trend, it's noise. On a base that small, a handful of impressions or one slow day moves the percentage that much. The most expensive mistake founders make is overhauling a healthy account because one week wobbled; you reset learning, lose your baselines, and create the very instability you were reacting to.

What would actually count as a signal: the same direction sustained for 3–4 weeks, or a swing big enough that it clearly can't be random — a CTR cut in half, conversions falling off a cliff, CAC moving 40–50%. A single −13% week is none of those.

So for now: leave it running, log the number, and look again next week. If it's still sliding three weeks from now, then we diagnose. Not before.

an0912.user: Logistics SaaS, last 30 days, post-iOS. Spend ₹10.5L. Here's my problem: Meta's dashboard says my ROAS is 3.7, but Shopify last-click is telling me 2.0. These two numbers don't agree and I genuinely can't tell which one is real. What's wrong with my setup?
an0912.assistant:
Nothing's wrong with your setup — you're just refereeing two scoreboards that are built to disagree, and waiting for them to match is a fight you'll never win.

Meta's 3.7 is its own modelled number: 7-day-click attribution, modelled conversions post-iOS, and a strong incentive to credit itself. Shopify's last-click 2.0 only crowns whoever the customer touched last, so it strips Meta of every assist it actually earned. Both are biased, in opposite directions. The truth sits somewhere between them — and neither dashboard will ever tell you where.

So stop trying to pick a winner. Anchor on blended CAC instead: total spend ÷ actual new customers. Take your ₹10.5L across all channels, divide by the real count of new customers Shopify recorded that month, and manage to that one number. It doesn't care which platform takes credit — it just tells you what a customer truly cost you.

From there, judge whether the business works on contribution per customer against that blended CAC. Platform ROAS becomes a directional signal for optimising inside Meta, nothing more. Caveat: blended CAC blurs channels together, so for incrementality you'd eventually want a geo holdout or a spend-down test — but as your day-to-day truth metric, blended is the one to trust.

an0917.user: Skincare brand, looking at last 30 days. Traffic's been decent — about 33,000 visits, roughly 3,111 added to cart, around 2,128 made it to checkout, and 635 actually purchased. CTR on the ads is 2.4%. Something feels off in the funnel but I can't put my finger on where the money's actually leaking.
an0917.assistant:
Your money's leaking at the very last step, and the numbers point straight at it.

Walk the funnel. 33,000 visits → 3,111 add-to-cart is 9.4% — healthy; people want the product. 3,111 → 2,128 reached checkout is fine too. But 2,128 reached checkout → 635 purchased is just 30%. That's the leak. A checkout-to-purchase rate should sit around 50–70%; yours is losing two of every three people who've already pulled out their wallet and walked to the till.

That's not an acquisition problem — your ads (2.4% CTR) and your product appeal (9.4% ATC) are doing their jobs. People intend to buy and then something stops them at payment. The usual culprits in Indian D2C: surprise shipping cost appearing at the last screen, a forced account-creation/login wall, or no UPI/COD option when most of your buyers want exactly that. Recover even half of that drop-off and you roughly double orders from 635 — with zero extra ad spend.

The lever: instrument the checkout and find where the 70% vanish. Watch session recordings of abandoned checkouts, check whether shipping/total reveals late, and make sure UPI and COD are front and centre. Leave the ad budget alone — it's not the problem. Caveat: confirm there isn't a tracking gap making purchases under-report (a misfiring pixel can fake a 30% rate); rule that out first so you're chasing a real leak, not a measurement artefact.

an0920.user: Pet-care brand, mostly SEO/organic driven but I've been scaling paid behind it. Over the last 8 weeks I pushed spend from ₹6L to ₹11.5L. The problem: as I scaled, CAC went from ₹570 to ₹1,004 and ROAS slid from 4.0 down to 2.3. AOV ₹2,300, margin 45%. I figured more budget = more growth but it's not really working. What's going on?
an0920.assistant:
What's going on is you've hit the channel's ceiling — and the contribution numbers show exactly when it stopped paying off. At the start: ₹2,300 × 45% − ₹570 = +₹465 per order. Now: ₹2,300 × 45% − ₹1,004 = +₹31 per order. You nearly doubled spend and squeezed your per-order profit down to almost nothing.

The mechanism is saturation. Your first ₹6L was buying your best, highest-intent audiences — the people most likely to buy pet-care from you. There's only a finite pool of those. Pushing to ₹11.5L meant the extra budget had to go fishing in colder, less-intent, pricier reach — so CAC climbed ₹570 → ₹1,004 and ROAS fell 4.0 → 2.3. More budget into the same finite pool doesn't grow it; it just bids up the leftovers.

The lever: create new demand before you add more budget. New audiences, new creative angles, new channels (Meta, WhatsApp, marketplace) — open up fresh pools instead of pouring more into the tapped-out one. Your job now is widening the top of the funnel, not pushing harder on a saturated one.

Caveat: 8 weeks of scaling can blur with seasonality or learning-phase resets — but a clean, monotonic CAC climb tracking your budget increases is the saturation signature, not noise. Hold spend at the efficient level while you build the next demand source.
